processing: A tea plant cultivar rather than a finished tea. Its leaf makes good black tea, processed by the usual withering, rolling, oxidation and drying.
harvest_season: Probably spring, as is usual; the source reports spring one-bud-two-leaf samples for analysis and says the buds stay tender for a good while, but gives no picking calendar.
appearance_dry: Depends on the tea made from it; as black tea, typically dark twisted strands.
appearance_liquor: As black tea, typically a clear reddish amber.
appearance_wet: Typically a coppery spent leaf, as with other Chinese black teas.
taste_profile: No tasting description specific to this cultivar is established beyond its reputation for good black tea; with fairly high polyphenols, expect some strength and briskness.

brewing.notes: General settings for a Chinese black tea, since this leaf rarely sells under its own name. Adjust to whatever the producer made from it.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under its own name, since it is a cultivar. Tea made from it follows its class, so black tea is usually sold from the current or previous year.
description:
Jianbohuang is a Chinese tea cultivar, not a tea you will usually see on a shelf. It was selected in Hunan from the old Anhua population of tea plants and is grown mainly in Hunan, with some planting in Jiangxi, Hubei, Henan and Anhui.

It is a semi-spreading bush of medium branching density. As a farmer's plant it has real weaknesses: modest budding vigour, low yield at around 70 kg per mu, weak adaptability and poor rooting from cuttings. Its strength is that the buds stay tender for a long time.

Its spring one-bud-two-leaf material tests at about 2.5% amino acids and 26.4% polyphenols, a profile that leans towards strength over sweetness. Its leaf has a name for making good black tea. No detailed tasting notes are established, so anything more would be a guess.

For most drinkers its main interest is as a parent: Jianbohuang No. 13 descends from it and fixed many of its weaknesses. If a Hunan producer names this cultivar, ask what class of tea they made from it.
history: The Tea Research Institute of the Hunan Academy of Agricultural Sciences developed it between 1957 and 1974 by single-plant selection from the Anhua population. It was then introduced to neighbouring tea provinces. Its seedling descendant, Jianbohuang No. 13, came from the same institute.
